take: The API’s reported 5.3 million barrel crude build, alongside substantial gasoline builds, sets a bearish near-term tone for flat price and reinforces the middle distillate tilt flagged by EIA, where refiners have shifted yields away from gasoline towards distillate and jet on elevated margins. In freight, the Hormuz crisis has handed US exporters of LNG, LPG and jet fuel a lasting advantage with new routes and multi-decade contracts, whilst China’s outbound dry bulk volumes have more than doubled since 2020, both of which lengthen tonne-miles and underpin freight. The inventory angle is unambiguous: a second consecutive weekly crude build per API normalises the US stock position just as Alaskan output is forecast to grow 13% in 2027, adding medium-term domestic supply. Watch the gasoil-bunker spread, with European gas inventories at their lowest pre-winter level in over a decade pulling LNG cargoes away from Asia and lifting European gas and LNG prices, which transmits into refining economics and bunker costs. The cross-market link to monitor is the African carbon charge programme on international shipping, which threatens another regional emissions regime layered onto existing ones and will feed directly into voyage costs and tonne-mile economics. Over the next 24 hours, watch the EIA weekly stocks data for confirmation of the API build, any escalation in the western Black Sea after the second serious merchant shipping incident off Bulgaria, and whether Apache’s North Sea production holds through the Unite walkouts involving around 170 offshore workers.
